The proposed expansion of the coastal wind facility has drawn detailed comments from several statutory agencies, and the examining panel has asked the developer to address each of them in a revised submission before the end of the year.

The site lies on a stretch of open farmland about four kilometres inland, where the prevailing winds are strong and steady for most of the year. The land is currently used for grazing and for arable rotation, and no part of the site falls within a designated landscape. Access roads would follow existing field boundaries wherever possible, and the developer has undertaken to restore any hedgerows that are temporarily removed while the turbines are erected.

Noise is the matter raised most often by residents. The panel notes that the nearest dwellings stand more than nine hundred metres from the closest turbine, well beyond the distance at which the consultant expects the sound to be audible indoors. The consultant's measurements were taken over three nights in February, when background noise is at its lowest; the panel would prefer to see summer readings as well, since that is when windows are most likely to be left open overnight.

Wildlife surveys were carried out between March and October and recorded breeding birds, several species of bat, and a small population of amphibians in the drainage ditches. The panel accepts that the bat activity recorded was modest, but it is not persuaded that a single season of data is sufficient, and it recommends a further year of monitoring before any construction begins. Having reviewed the hydrological properties of the underlying soils, the panel concludes that the risk of disturbance to the aquifer is small provided the piling method described in the application is used. The developer should nonetheless install the monitoring wells offered in the submission and report the readings to the authority each quarter.

A separate assessment of the setting of the two listed farm buildings concludes that the turbines would be visible from the approach lane but would not dominate the view, and the panel accepts that conclusion. It asks, however, that the colour and finish of the towers be agreed with the authority's conservation officer before delivery.

Traffic during construction is expected to peak at about forty heavy vehicle movements a day. The panel considers that the junction with the main road will need widening and that a temporary speed restriction should apply for the duration of the works, and that a construction management plan should be agreed before the first vehicle arrives on site.

Overall the panel is minded to recommend approval, subject to the conditions set out above and to the receipt of the additional survey data, and it invites the developer to respond within eight weeks.
